utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Case number IT-97-25-T, the Prosecutor versus Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Who is it who wishes to raise something? Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Prosecution would like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm sorry, I haven't got any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Can you hear me now in a language which you understand? You are not the accused. It's all right. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, after discussion with the Defence yesterday, we have several matters solved. First of all, the Prosecution would like to tender into evidence some documents related to Witness 33. These documents are actually in the trial binder, but it has to be officially handed over. It is in the trial binder, it is -- first of all, the transcript of this witness, in the trial binder, it's ID 106. That's the transcript of Witness 33's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: During the testimony, several documents were discussed with this witness. First of all, there was a map the witness produced, a map of Foca, and this is in the trial -- it is in the trial binders. The document, let me just see, is 99, ID 99. And we have the documents provided by the witness, the exit permits for herself and the family. Those are the documents with the identification number ID 100 to ID 104A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. 100. What's the next one?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: 100 to 104A, that is, 100 and 100A, 101, 101A, 102, 102A, 103, 103A, and 104, 104A. These were the exit permits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just let me get that right. There's 100, 101, 101A, 102, 103, 103A, 104, and 104A.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: There are also 100A and 102A. All these documents, 100 to 104, have also a translation which is A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Those documents go in under seal, as well as the map because the map also shows the name of the witness. The last exhibit that came in was the witness statement, the previous witness statement to the Prosecutor's Office. That was tendered also under seal from the Defence. It is document ID 96. We would like to enter these documents now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, those documents will be Exhibit P106 --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm so sorry. I just have to be sure. Document 96 is a statement given to the Prosecution or, rather, the investigators of the OTP in relation to this witness; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And it was tendered into evidence in the other trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: By the Defence counsel, actually, and it's discussed in the transcript at various points.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then there are no objections whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I just want to mention that in the testimony of this witness, several videos were shown. We did not enter them here because the videos were actually discussed intensely during the testimony, and the contents of the video are to be seen from the testimony itself. So it's just not necessary to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Those will be Exhibits P106, and then the following ones are under seal: P99, 100, 100A, 101, 101A, 102, 102A, 103, 103A, 104, 104A, and 96.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. We have also discussed the matter of summoning of this one witness, and the Defence and the Prosecution agree that the witness should be summoned like it is requested but not for the 26th of February but at an earlier stage, that is, the 13th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So the summons is issued by consent. Can you provide us with a document to sign?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, we can do that. Yes. I don't have it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no, but if you have it during the morning, then it could be signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We'll do so. We have also reached an agreement on the Witness 96, but we will come back to this at a later stage. We will have to strike some of the parts of it and we have to agree on this first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well then.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I wonder if the motion of the Defence should be discussed now with the request for examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm afraid that I have not yet received any document identifying the precise issue. It may be lost in the Registry's interstices, but they certainly have not been supplied to the Trial Chamber yet. So I think we better wait until we see that. Anything else before we bring the witness back in?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Anything else, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Let's have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, Witness. Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Examined by Mr. Smith: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Witness, I just have a few more questions to ask you this morning, and as we discussed yesterday, if it -- it would be appreciated if you could specifically listen carefully to the question and specifically answer the question, and if any extra further information is required another question will follow, but listen very specifically to the question that's asked. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you gave some evidence that Zulfo Veiz was taken out of your room at about 9.00 and taken down to the administration building, and then you heard some beatings and some screaming coming from that building about ten minutes after he was taken out. You said that the beatings and the screamings lasted for about half an hour to an hour. Then I asked you, "Did you hear anything else after this beating or screaming?" And you said that was one of the last things that happened. Following the screaming and the beatings, did you hear anything else that was connected to this particular incident?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that very late in the night, between 11.00 and 12.00 at night. I mean, between 2300 and 2400 hours. I heard the squeaking of brakes or, rather, wheels, and bursts of gunfire from weapons. Approximately about ten minutes later a loud sound was heard, the thump of something falling into the Drina. This could be heard well because it was about 200 metres away as the crow flies, and the silence was such we say that it was as silent as in a cemetery or in the grave. I had the impression that I could see all of this although I could not see it. I could hear and feel that this could have been his end. I'm referring to Zulfo Veiz.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many bursts of gunfire did you hear?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, usually these were intermittent shots, two or three, depending on how many persons there were for that night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this night, after Zulfo Veiz was taken out, have you ever seen him again?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of him being alive since that night?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But people who were with me in the camp from that room asked one of the guards, "What's up with Zulfo?" The guard said, "He's been transferred to another camp."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned that this type of incident that occurred to Zulfo Veiz occurred to a number of other detainees who were taken out over a one- to two-month period from the dormitory and taken to the administration building. You said that some people were taken three or four times a week and sometimes it was just once a week, and you said you had to place a pillow over your ears to block out the screams. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Within about two months' time, what happened to Zulfo Veiz happened to many others, whether it's 40, 50, 60, whatever. But these people were usually taken before night would fall, at 6.00, 7.00, or 8.00, and after that, such terrible screams and moans could be heard from that direction that I would take a sponge instead of cotton wool to put into my ears. And even that couldn't keep the sound out. I even had to put my pillow over my head so that this would not reach my ears and so that I would not be so ill because of all those screams.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned, after Zulfo Veiz was taken to the administration building, that there was gunfire and then the thump of his body into the -- the thump of what appeared to be a body into the river. Did gunfire occur after other beatings that you've just referred to, or was it just in relation to Zulfo Veiz?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same happened to the others who were taken out for beatings and the same procedure was involved, approximately the same; the squeaking of brakes or, rather, wheels, then a very short trip. And in a relatively short period of time, it depended on how many people had to be finished off, there were intermittent bursts of gunfire that lasted longer, in relation to Zulfo, that is. On the assumption that this night between the 20st and 21st of August, as far as I can remember, Zulfo was taken away in the evening, and four, five, six times, a loud splash could be heard, loud splashes of something falling into the water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how many people were taken to the administration building over this period that you've just mentioned and appeared to be beaten in this way? Can you give an approximate number?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that lasted for about two months. As far as that period is concerned, I haven't got any precise records, but 40, 50, or even 60 people finished in that way. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "finished in that way," you've stated that 40 or 50 or 60 people were beaten in that way. How many of those people came back into the KP Dom after those beatings?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who generally was committing these beatings? Who was doing -- who was committing these assaults in the administration centre?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. But according to information previously received, it was the military police that contributed to this the most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These particular people that were taken out and beaten in the administration building, were they selected for any particular reason over and above other detainees?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, to the best of our knowledge, "special treatment" was accorded to members of the SDA, persons who worked in the municipal authorities, persons who had worked in the police before, as well as persons who were organised in some kind of SDA logistics. At least that's what people said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How well known amongst the prisoners, amongst the detainees, was this practice of beating and subsequent hearing of shots?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everybody heard it. Part of the detainees would see them leave but no one would see these men return. Ninety-nine per cent of all detainees could hear these screams.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This practice of people being taken out and beaten and never being seen again, what effect did that have on you whilst you were in prison?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very hard. I don't know what the right term for this would be, but it was horror.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than these people that you mentioned were taken into the administration building and beaten, were there other detainees that appeared to have disappeared from the KP Dom whilst you were there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was, as they say, "legal," under quotation marks. Certain groups would go to pick plums or to do other things in groups of 10 or 15, which later did not return at all, nor did we receive any information as to what had happened with them. But only later it turned out that they were out on a road of no return.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than the detainees that you've mentioned that were beaten in the administration centre, how many -- can you put a number as to the amount of detainees that were at the KP Dom whilst you were there and were never seen again afterwards? If you're unable to say, just say so.

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our records -- records were kept every day because we went in the direction of the restaurant for about 100 metres, and I said in my statement that sometimes one or two groups would be brought together as they went out. We knew every day how many people there were within the camp. We also knew how many people were in solitary confinement. In my assessment, between 700 and 800 people had passed through the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the time that you were there, did you have any assessment as to how many people were missing after being in the camp? Only from the time that you were there.

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period about 100 persons disappeared. Perhaps 110 or 115 even, but around 100.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does this include the people that were beaten in the administration building in the evening or is that number on top of that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is the total number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just ask that the witness be given P55. Not to go through it in any detail but just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Schedule C.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Schedule C. It's just to clarify one name that was there yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I just ask that you look at the piece of paper in front of you and look at number C17. The person's name is Krunoslav Marinovic.

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 17.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that person at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him from before. He had a workshop of his own, a repair shop for radio and TV sets, but I saw him at the KP Dom on the 19th and 20th. His face was totally distorted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 19th and 20th of which month?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: April. April 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we discussed this person yesterday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour, the person was discussed as Kresimir Martinovic, which appears to be probably a pronunciation problem on my part.

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This person, he received injuries to his face. Did he receive them in the KP Dom or before he arrived there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came back with these injuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He came to the KP Dom with those injuries?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know what happened to him after you saw him on the 19th or 20th of April?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said to the people around him -- I mean, I personally did not ask him, but it was Ostojic's escorts who had beaten him so badly that they had trouble bringing him to the KP Dom. They mutilated his face. He was treated with cold compresses only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd just like to ask you just a couple of questions about your attempted exchange whilst you were at the KP Dom and then your final exchange when you left. I think it was on the 17th of June, 1992, about 12 to 15 prisoners from KP Dom were taken to or near to Cajnice.

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that date correct or could --

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in mid-July. I don't really remember whether it was the 17th or the 18th, but it was the middle of July 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were taken there with a van full of women and some children and some elderly males; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were taken. There were six from Gorazde and there were about ten of us from Foca, so about 12 to 16 altogether. We rode in a lorry, and children, two old men of about 80, and two or three women of about the same age came there, and there was also a rather young nurse there and about ten children between the ages of three and six or seven.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These children, the two or three women and the two old men, where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second night -- the first night we spent in a school at Miljevina, and the second night, after the failed exchange, we were transferred to the school at Luke. That night we were lying on benches on the upper floor, we were all together there, and I learned from that nurse that they had been transferred from an auxiliary camp called Partizan and brought there for exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that nurse tell you how they were treated at the Partizan camp?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a story that I simply could not believe because it defied imagination. Soldiers would go there from time to time, take those women away and do most despicable things to them. The most despicable things are those which are physical, without any emotions, and which end in a lifelong trauma for those women.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you talking about rapes?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this exchange failed and you were taken back to the KP Dom, and the women and children were taken back to Partizan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who notified you that you were going to be exchanged on that occasion? Was it guards, was it soldiers, or was it someone else? When you were first taken out of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A group had arrived from, I guess, the military part of Cajnice, and they tried to use us to retrieve their own men who were in prisons or perhaps in an area, to have them exchanged for those of us who were in the Gorazde territory. The one who was in charge of that organisation - I don't know him; I never knew him - he told us that he used to be a school teacher in Cajnice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you taken from your room at the KP Dom by guards and then delivered to soldiers at the front of the KP Dom, or did soldiers come to your room? Who escorted you out through the KP Dom on your way for this attempted exchange?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our guards first searched us in two places to see if we were carrying something and they searched us very thoroughly, from head to feet, so that we could not really take over anything of any suspicious nature, even in a written form, let alone an object. We were turned over to men from Cajnice in the building itself, and then they told us to begin boarding a lorry. There was also some Vojvoda from Cajnice who immediately started to threaten us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then if we can move to the 29th of August. I think about 55 detainees from the KP Dom, including yourself, were taken towards Niksic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. In the morning of the 28th, the guard Obrenovic came to the door and had a list with him, and I was one of those on the list so I was called out last. We were both happy and unhappy. But we heard from him something that we did not believe right away, because he told us we were going to the free territory of Yugoslavia. We did not know because some men were picked out from every dormitory. This selection usually meant either youth or very advanced-aged men with some health complaints. On the 28th of August, that is, that same day, we were transferred to a room and there we waited for about ten hours for a bus which did not turn up. We were then taken back to Room 12.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told that you were going to be exchanged or released?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told that we would be released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given a choice as to where you were going to be released?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The following day, the 55 of you headed off in the bus. On that journey, did you come across a Pero Elez?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day, when we started off in a bus, we waited a long time in front of various institutions which were to give us a green light, that is, issue us different papers allowing us to move on. So after several such stops, we set off, after some harassment on the border with Montenegro. Along the way, we were also harassed up to a certain point by the army of Republika Srpska; not those escorting us but those who stopped us. We were all merry to have passed through all that, and arrived some 5 or 6 kilometres from Niksic. Niksic is in Montenegro. In Montenegro, the driver automatically stopped and said, "We have to go back." What happened? Pero Elez, whom they called Vojvoda, turned us all back to the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What function did Pero Elez have at the KP Dom? Was he involved in the KP Dom at all? Was he in the army? Do you know what role he had at this time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was one of the important Vojvoda in the territory of Miljevina, and as such, I suppose he wielded a lot of influence, had an Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. important say with the Crisis Staff and other officials. He and another one turned the bus back, and you can well imagine what authority he enjoyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, we've heard an awful lot about Pero Elez in various cases, but I've never heard that phrase "Vojvoda" before. Could we get some understanding what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, excuse me. Before we move on, the witness said, "Can you imagine what kind of military authority he had," and it is not in the transcript. I think it is very important. I know that it will be checked the next day, but it is rather important, so I wanted to make a point of that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. But can we find out what that phrase means, what that word means, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Pero Elez was an important Vojvoda in the territory of Miljevina. What do you mean by the term "Vojvoda"?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Vojvoda" is a title which dates back to old times, to the historical times in the history of the warfare of these people. A person with this title, I cannot say exactly what rank, that means in military terms, but it is a military rank, and it ensures -- it vests that person with authority in a particular setting. May I add? In that place in Serbia where I was finally fetched up from the International Red Cross and Crescent, I received something similar. Pero Elez, Vojvoda of Miljevina, took a freight, that is a passenger, that is, a car from the International Red Cross, and all the documentation, including the record of us all, towards the end of April and the beginning of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Pero Elez was in the Bosnian Serb military in the Foca area at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said the driver said that the bus had to go back to the KP Dom. Was the driver from the KP Dom or was he a soldier from --

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wore civilian clothes and was very decent. No sooner had we crossed the border when he addressed us warmly, "Well, you need not be afraid any more. We are in a different republic." But that proved to be a mistake. He used to work earlier for a shipping company as a bus driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pero Elez caused for the bus to go back to the KP Dom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear why he caused the bus to go back to the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because we did not communicate with them, with him. He ordered the driver to turn the bus back and that is how it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the bus arrived back at the KP Dom, and were 20 people from that bus segregated from the 55?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were turned back, and we were offered then, because we had not eaten, to eat something. So we went to the restaurant and returned from the restaurant all together to Room 11. Half an hour later, a guard came and he had a list with him, and he called out -- he started calling out and called about 20 men. I was not among them. I thought that those that he was calling out perhaps had some advantage. So I ran up to them and the guard says, "What do you want? What are you waiting here?" And I said, "Well, am I not there?" And he said, "Just beat it."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to these 20 men? Where did they go?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, some 20 minutes perhaps, half an hour later, the same guard came and told us to get ready quickly. We did get ready quickly and then the same procedure started all over again. And again the same procedure through one gate, through another gate, search, no particular problems, and we boarded the same bus once again. It just happened so that I turned to the right across the River Drina and I saw a bus full of people. Assumption, my assumption, is that those people had either taken the old road towards Miljevina or the road to Gorazde, that is, Ustikolina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which people are you referring to? Are you referring to the 20 that were selected whilst you were in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I am referring to them. I had an intuition that it could only be they, even though I could not, of course, recognise them at that distance. But there was some intuition that those men could have been them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see those 20 in fact being taken out of the KP Dom or not?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it --

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, they were taken from the room. I saw them go through this second door which leads into the main lobby of the administrative building, and after that we lost them from sight, which means they had left the facility. I could see them go through the door which is used under normal conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the names of any of these individuals that were in this group of 20?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was particularly close to, and on the 28th I spent most of my time with him while we waited in the bus for those eight hours, and we talked if we left whom to communicate, how to find people, because one doesn't really think very much if he gets out to the free territory whom to find and how. So it was Ismet Pasovic who was particularly close to me. At that time, he was close to 70.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in that group of 20 that was selected?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the names of any other individuals that were in that group of 20 that were selected by the guard?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did sort of register it somewhere. But, I mean, there was a Granov who used to be a social worker and worked for the same company as I did. There were some from Gorazde. A man who -- there was Esad Nezbur. There was that other one from Gorazde who hoped that his wife might be able to get him out of there because she had some rather good connections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to these 20 individuals that were taken out?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, later one learnt, naturally, that a man cannot sleep easily unless he pursues truth. But to come by such information, to learn what happened to whom, that is very difficult, very difficult. But at the same time, after all this time, I committed myself to it, both wishing to help those who had remained behind me. So I tried to do what I could. I could not come by any information about what happened to them. They are simply not among the living anymore - that is something that I know for certain - because to this day I have not received any indication that they are still alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've stated to the Court that you were detained at the KP Dom for four and a half months, and you've stated to the Court what you saw there and how you were treated. How has that affected you today psychologically?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like many others, I experienced some hard moments after I came out because freedom was highly hazardous wherever. I received treatment in a number of hospitals. I also went to different institutions, from physical therapists to psychologists, and I was also received in different health institutions so as to allay, as much as I could, the trauma that I still feel. I'm still under medical observation by specialists in psychology and other institutions which want to help me. As time goes by, it becomes ever harder because one does not see any chance for one's personal future or the future of one's family, and that leaves a very deep mark on my soul. I see no future and no money, no money, no property which could, as we say it in Bosnia, "rahatluk," give us peace which we enjoyed before the war broke out. Everybody was looked after; everybody had his plans and thought about his future.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Cross-examined by Mr. Bakrac:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wish you good morning, Witness. My name is Mihajlo Bakrac, and I'm one of the defenders of the accused Milorad Krnojelac. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, Witness, that you told the investigators of the Prosecution, on the 13th and 14th of November, 1995 and on the 27th and 29th of May and the 4th of June, 1999, your statements?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct, if I remember the dates correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make those statements of your own free will, and did you sign them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that in your statement of the 27th and 29th of May and the 4th of June, 1999, on page 5, passage 7, you stated the following, verbatim: "Krnojelac was de jure the commander/warden of the KP Dom, but the power de facto was in the hands of Todovic, Rasevic, and the military police."

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Bakrac. Witness, when you are answering a question asked of you by Mr. Bakrac, you must realise that because you are both speaking in the same language, the translator has a little bit of trouble keeping up with you. So would you please pause before you answer to enable the translators to catch up with the end of the sentence. Just a short pause and then they will be able to pick up the whole of your answer. So far they have been very short answers; but if you give a longer one, it may be difficult to keep up with you if you go on straight away.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you said in your statement to the Prosecutor, that is, to the Prosecutor's investigators, and which we have just read, is quite true.

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that in one of those statements you also said that on the 3rd of May, 1992, a delegation of the International Red Cross, which included two Swiss citizens, registered you as a prisoner in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I pronounced the date, the 3rd of May, 1992, ten days or so after your detention.

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot really be sure if it was the 3rd of May. But as far as I can remember, that was the very end of April and the beginning of May. But to the best of my recollection, it could be -- I don't know if it is important, but it could have been on the 30th of April or perhaps on the 1st. It was then that those people from the International Red Cross came with two girls who were interpreters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we can agree that it was about ten days or so after your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. detention.

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also correct that in one of your statements you said that on the day when you last talked to Milorad Krnojelac, at the end of that conversation, Savo Todovic said to you that you should go and give a statement to the press?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, it is correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is correct that it is not the accused Krnojelac who directed you to do so but that it was Savo Todovic who told you to go and speak to the press, give a statement to the press?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, please be so kind as to tell me the following: You said here before the Tribunal that you had four contacts with Mr. Krnojelac. Can you remember whether these are the last -- the only moments when you saw Mr. Krnojelac at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, these are not the only moments. Like all the others, I saw him through the window, I saw him passing by through the yard, because that was the only way to go from the exit to the furniture factory or, rather, the restaurant and also to the area where the cooking was done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Tell me, please, is it correct that you said to the investigators of the OTP that you saw Mr. Krnojelac during regular working hours, until about 4.00 in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to the best of my recollection, I think that Krnojelac was there, for the most part, during working hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "during working hours," what period is this?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether it's four or three or five, but that was what their working hours were, and the guard shift was around 6.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about the main leaders of the Serb Democratic Party. Can you tell me who the main leaders for the SDA in Foca were?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could say that in 1991 a certain differentiation had already started in terms of the presentation of candidates on the part of parties. I think Taib Lojo was appointed president of the municipality by the SDA. I think they held certain functions, certain posts in that sense. In 1991 or perhaps even earlier - I wasn't very well-versed, to tell you the truth - they divided certain posts, certain offices, the SDA and the SDS did, but I know that in Foca, Sahinpasic, nicknamed Saja, was in charge of Republican activity and he was a Republican MP. As for the others, quite frankly, I had work to do, to tell you the truth, so I was not very much involved in who was doing what and how.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. It's a bit strange to me. You are very well-versed in the leaders of the SDS, and when I speak about the leaders of the SDA, you were very busy, you were not interested. How come that's possible for you to know so little about the leaders of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a citizen, I was 100 per cent neutral. I did not belong to any party. I -- I mean, at that time it was relatively normal to belong to the League of Communists. At that time, sometime in 1989, I stopped being a member of that organisation, and from then onwards, I did not belong to any political party. For those reasons, I can say who the members were, but quite frankly speaking, I cannot say whether such-and-such a person was a member of the SDA and what post he held. However, I can say who held which office. Reuf Tafra was director of the regional medical centre. Whether he belonged to the SDA or whether it was the SDA that appointed him to that position, I cannot go into that at all, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Please be so kind as to say whether you know who was commander of the Territorial Defence just before the conflict broke out in Foca and what was his ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it should have been Sulejman Pilav.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is he ethnically?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a Muslim, a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned Mr. Sahinpasic, nicknamed Saja. Yesterday you said that Serbs were arming themselves but Muslims were too. Do you know that Sahinpasic stated in parliament and the newspapers that already in 1991 and 1992 he was arming Muslims in Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know at all of him doing that? Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only when I came to a certain country, republic of the former Yugoslavia, that I found out about the activities of that man. It was very negative in terms of persons of Muslim ethnicity. This man you mentioned, Saja, it is true that he was a MP, but I did not know anything about the arming of the Muslim part of the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned in your statement yesterday that you were present at the SDS rally which was held at the stadium in Foca, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that before this rally, a rally of the Party of Democratic Action was held in Foca.

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that on the stage, when we are talking about the rally of the Serb Democratic Party at the stadium, you saw the main people from the SDS at republican level. Can you tell us who was on the stage together with them from Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Originally from Foca it was Ostojic, Maksimovic, as far as I can remember. My visual memory is relatively good, so I go through this reconstruction quite a different way. Then there was Stanic. There was someone else too, but that -- that image comes back to me from the second row. I cannot reconstruct that part of the image. Cancar. Yes, Petko Cancar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Yesterday, you said when you came to the KP Dom -- you said that when you came to the KP Dom that a person nicknamed Cakani registered your name in the logbook there and that you cannot remember his last name. Would you agree if I said that that person's last name is Dobnik and that he is an ethnic Croat?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that -- I mean, I'm sure that he was Nedjo Klaric's brother or son-in-law, brother-in-law or son-in-law, but I would not have known that he was of Catholic ethnicity. I know that he worked there as a corrections officer, but, quite frankly, I never gave much thought to his last name. But I know 100 per cent that he was Nedjo Klaric's son-in-law or brother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note the word is ambiguous in the original, whether it's "son-in-law" or "brother-in-law."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You may not have heard what the interpreters said there. There is an ambiguity in the word which the witness is using as to whether it means his brother-in-law or his son-in-law. You may or may not want to follow that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you used this word "zet," is that the man's sister's husband or the man's daughter's husband? You heard what was said by the Honourable Judge.

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our jargon, it means that he got married to Nedjo Klaric's daughter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So it's son-in-law. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just reading from the list of staff members from the KP Dom, and I'm asking you whether you would agree that the person nicknamed Cakani is that person, that is, Aleksandar Dobnik, father's name, Rudolf, born in 1944. He worked in security.

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say for sure whether that's his name and surname officially, but I know 100 per cent sure that his nickname was Cakani. He had great respect for me. That day, when he registered all my details, he offered me a cigarette and he also gave me a pack of cigarettes without the filter. The brand is Niska Morava.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. When speaking of medical care, you said that at first, once a week, and later, once in 15 or 20 days, doctors/physicians came from the medical centre of Foca. Is it correct that in the KP Dom, Gojko Jokanovic, a male nurse, was there every day, and isn't that what you said in your statements to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, I stated that, but I'm sorry that I did not state - I remembered this later - that instead of a doctor, instead of a general practitioner or an occupational medicine specialist, we had a gynaecologist coming in to see us. I'm not saying this was every day, but almost every day, in the KP Dom building, Gojko Jokanovic was there. He retired as a medical technician, as a male nurse, from the KP Dom, and he was reactivated when the concentration camp was set up in Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also correct that a dentist, Boban Kostovic, was also at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, once or twice during my period. Let me add one more thing. He did not have any chance of intervening in any way, not extracting a tooth either, because these premises were devastated. He only gave Aspirin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that what you know about this or is that what you say was the case for sure?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assert that that is the way it was, 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Speaking of medical care, do you know that someone in your room received an infusion?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But semilegally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that you were present when there was a clash between Mr. Krnojelac and the commander of the Uzice Corps, let's call it that; when Krnojelac, in your opinion, phoned the Crisis Staff and, in your opinion, talked to Stanic. Do you allow for the possibility that, on that occasion, Mr. Krnojelac talked to Mr. Radojica Mladzenovic, President of the Executive Council?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot assert what the name was and I cannot say whether this was the commander or the commanding officer. But I know that he had some kind of high authority, order-issuing authority over Krnojelac, the one who insisted that he, Krnojelac, use that number to make a phone call. According to my visual memory, that's the way I recorded it. Now, how accurate this was, I don't know. I remember the number as being 570041. Perhaps it's my tragedy that I have this visual memory. Although this time distance is so long, I tried to record this earlier. I think that the name could be Stanic, because he was President of the SDS. Stanic could also be President of the Crisis Staff. So I'm not claiming what the name was exactly, but I do claim that it could be the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke of a cafe that was in the family home of Mr. Krnojelac. Did you ever go there? Did you ever spend any time in that cafe? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When his son designed the interior - he did so himself, his son did - he put in some kind of decorative objects. I dropped in then, and if I'm not mistaken, I was invited for a drink one more time as a neighbour, of course. I must tell you that I was pleased that such a man did quite a few things like that by himself. I was even surprised. But let me tell you quite frankly, in terms of my job, the job I had, I was supposed to communicate with quite a few persons from the business community, so I was kind of fed up with restaurants and cafes. This is an unwritten rule, that business people go out to eat and drink together after business meetings. I never went to restaurants and cafes except on exceptional occasions. I was not interested in that, regardless of who the owner was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you say that nationalist, chauvinist songs were sung in that cafe, you had never actually entered it.

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not listen to it, but I heard from neighbours in that street that, late into the night, songs were sung of a nationalist content.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know that right next to that cafe, about 30 metres away, there is a cafe with a live band owned by Grujicic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you allow for the possibility that these nationalist songs were heard precisely from that locality?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said a few minutes ago, I was not the one who listened to these songs. So if the neighbours say that that's the way it was, my ad hoc reaction was to accept that, which is not to say that something like that did not happen in the next-door cafe, the Grujicic family place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you did not come to the cafe that was held by Mr. Krnojelac's son, do you allow for the possibility, or were you told by the neighbours that, just before the conflict broke out, persons of Muslim ethnicity also came to that cafe?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I should not be telling you all of this because I assume that you were one of the persons surrounded by various members of the population and various friends. It would be illogical for me to say that they did not come. They did come. Before the conflict broke out, all ethnic groups socialised, especially young men. It would be an idiocy, undoubtedly, to deny that, that they did not come to see each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. When we are talking about ethnicity, do you know what is the ethnicity of Mr. Krnojelac's wife, the mother of his sons?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying I'm right, but as far as I can remember, his wife is a good mother, a good worker, and I think that she is from a Catholic family, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps this would be a good point to take a break. I have a few more questions. I'm not going to be very long but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Certainly. Thank you very much. We'll adjourn now until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. If I could just have a brief word. During the break, the interpreter advised me that the witness had difficulty hearing the interpretation, so I asked the usher if he could turn up his volume. So hopefully there should be no problems now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday in your testimony you mentioned some people and told us that they had been battered. Could you now, if you can tell me, and I shall give you names one by one, which rooms were they kept in? Mr. Munib Veiz.

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Munib Veiz was in Room 11 when he arrived. Whether he arrived on the 18th or the 19th, but I saw him there. On the 19th it was Room 2 -- no, excuse me, Room 11, which included -- in department 11, which included four rooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Nurko Nisic.

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nurko Nisic was not in our department, in number 19. He was also in the Room 11, but it happened later. And other things also happened later when many of those who had been in Room 11 and 12 and 15 left to another facility, an adjacent facility under the same roof but with a different entrance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, to make it quite clear and quite precise, at the time when they were taken away, which room were they taken away from and which room were they returned to?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were taken from Room 12 and brought back to Room 12, that is, the department. That is what we called it. But those departments had several rooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I understand that. Thank you. When you say taken away and brought back to Room 12, it concerns Mr. Munib Veiz and Mr. Nurko Nisic, does it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mustafa Kuloglija.

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mustafa Kuloglija - you pronounced it wrongly as Kologlija but he's Kuloglija - he was in that same facility with the common entrance, and he was in Room 12. That was the quarantine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mandzo.

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the other facility. At first there was a collective, that is, all the prisoners were in one facility with one entrance, but as their number grew, as the number of inmates grew, other rooms were opened with another entrance which could not be properly controlled, that is, one could not see who came in or out. When he returned, Mandzo was in the same facility as I was. I don't know which room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To make it quite clear, tell us, during the relevant period when they were coming back from beatings, what room were you in?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in 15, a somewhat smaller room than other rooms. There were seven or eight people, depending on the number of beds that could fit in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally, Mr. Konjo, what room was he taken from and brought back to?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Konjo was in Room 12, which was called the quarantine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you told us and today you were asked by the Prosecutor specifically that Mr. Krunoslav Marinovic had been brought beaten to the KP Dom. My question is to try to clarify it. When you spoke about Mr. Nail Hodzic, was he also brought to the KP Dom beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was brought there beaten, I mean, Nail Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Omer Mujezinovic, had he also been beaten already when he arrived in KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Omer Mujezinovic. I don't remember. Perhaps Uzunovic. It could be a mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know an individual called Omer Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Perhaps by sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Omer Mujezinovic, was he beaten at all? Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really say whether I know him or whether I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Zulfo Veiz. Was he also brought to the KP Dom beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean he arrived beaten at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you testified that there was a room from which you heard the sounds of beating and that that room had window panes painted over; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the windows open or closed when that went on?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The windows were shut, but one could glean the outlines of people, silhouettes, through those shut windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I should like to ask the usher to help us to give the witness the ground plan, and I'd like to ask the witness to show us the room from which those sounds reached them.

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be the ground floor, a relatively large room, and I claim that that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the sake of the transcript, I shall try to explain what the witness showed. On the ground plan, ID 6/1, the witness is pointing at the right-hand part of the administrative building, the fourth room marked as "Sala," as "hall." S-a-l-a. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the same ground plan, could you show me where is the room that you were in and on what floor is that room.

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the ground plan. So the Room 15 was about this size, and it had an entrance in front of the lavatory, then another door which was roughly this size of the common room and the whole length like this. There were about 25 to 30 beds, and here in this part there was a room with two windows with six, seven, eight beds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: As he was pointing, although on document 6/1, if you look at 6/4, he was identifying Room 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much for your assistance. That, I believe, quite suffices to identify, please, the things shown by the witness. Since Room 15 actually included four rooms, I will now ask the usher to take Exhibit 6/4 and then the witness can show us which one of those four rooms he was in.

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've forgotten. I was in -- I was in -- rather, I slept, I had a bed in this room here, and it had windows here and here. It had a fantastic view; that is, if you wanted to look through the window at this part, and then you could go to here because it also had two windows in front of the lavatory, and you could see this side. So this drawing is a caricature of a drawing because the view was much better from here. So this is not a good drawing because it should have been like this. This is one dormitory, this is the third dormitory, and then between that one and next to this one, there was a common room, and then a wall. Then in this part, there was another room, 5 by 6 metres or about a 20- or 30-metre area, and then the entrance into the dormitory. So a room in front of the lavatory, then a common room; then from this common room, one entered this room with some 25 to 30 beds and this smaller one with two windows which had seven or maybe eight cots. This one overlooked the walls, and this one, four or six windows altogether, with a view of this area here, like this. So from here, we could see as far as this, and here they had the power generator. We could also observe this part here. We could not see this here, that is, the entrance into the canteen. So we could directly see what went on from here, that is, in this direction, and everything around the gate. I think this explanation suffices. And you should correct this drawing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The room which he pointed to was the right-hand Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. bottom room within the group of rooms described as Room 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for your help. I was about to specify it for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question is as follows: Today you told us that you spent four and a half months in the KP Dom, and that on various occasions when you heard beatings, you also heard bursts of fire. Were those the only times when you heard a shot or shots in the vicinity of the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In daytime, when they would be coming from the battlefield, I guess, there would be some gunfire but very little. At night there was hardly any other gunfire except this one, at least in the vicinity. Therefore, I'd need, perhaps, a little more time to paint for you that picture of what it looked like. Between the exit, as they call it chronologically, it happened as of 6.00 or 7.00 p.m. until about 12.00 or half past twelve or 1.00 at night. If the Court permits and if the Chamber wants me to, I can, I believe, describe very graphically the cries of pain, screams, dull blows, with intermittent bursts of fire around half past eleven, 12.00, half past twelve. Screeches, whether it was a Lada car, and I know the sound of the engine, or whether it was a Golf. But one of those two vehicles, I'm 100 per cent sure, took away those half-dead people from the administrative people in the direction of the bridge. I did not see that, but I have, I'm certain to this day, I have this 100 per cent clear image as to how these things happened. If you want me to explain further, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. Please tell me, how far is it from the main gate of the KP Dom to the bridge on the Drina?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you it down to the last metre, but I can tell you that it could be about 70 or maybe 80 metres from the main gate, or even, I would allow, perhaps 100 metres. It's more difficult to say, as the crow flies. But from our room, it could not have been more than 100, 120, or I'll allow 150 metres, as the crow flies, to the beginning of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you agree with me that the Drina is a mountain river and that one can hear it, that it has its own rumble?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how familiar with geography you are, but I guess you are not particularly familiar with geography. If the Drina were a mountain river, people would never be able to swim in it. The Drina was a major magnet for people from the continent to come and swim in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that the investigators simulated the throwing of bodies from the bridge and that it could not be heard in the KP Dom? Are you quite sure that what you heard was the throwing of bodies into the river?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, simulation or no simulation, but, sir, had you been in my shoes, had you been in my place, you would have also created in your mind an image such as the one that I am describing. You wouldn't have had a slightest doubt if it was simulation or reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Smith:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned to my learned friend that in a previous statement made to an investigator at the Tribunal, that you described Mr. Krnojelac as having de jure power and Mr. Rasevic and Mr. Todovic as having de facto power. Were they the terms that you used?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what you mean by de jure power, Mr. Krnojelac's de jure power?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: De jure means legally; de facto means in reality. So, and that is my opinion, he was the warden who performed those duties which were within his jurisdiction; but de facto, in reality, larger powers in the discharge of certain duties were vested in those two that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who vested those powers in those two people that you mentioned, Mr. Rasevic and Mr. Todovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think - I cannot, of course, say that this is indeed so - but I think that it was the type of organisation, that it was simply a form of organisation in which the Crisis Staff, which was on the outside but nevertheless had a major influence, and also the military police played a major role. So, organisationally speaking, the functioning of all that, those two had more control than a man who was the warden.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that sense, are you saying that they exercised the power of the warden? Is that what you're saying, or is it something else?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's something along those lines. I cannot really say for certain what the internal organisation was. But I'm referring to people who were carrying out not the policy but what was to be done with inmates, whether it was in the organisational sense of the word or perhaps some other - security, maltreatment, solitary confinement, so on and so forth. But I think that those two were carrying out the tasks that had been given them. Who had given them, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you stated that Mr. Krnojelac was the warden. What responsibilities did he have? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of his responsibilities or powers. I know that he was the warden of the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's the Defence case that Mr. Krnojelac was only in charge of the economic facility and not in charge of the detention of the Muslim detainees. Do you have an opinion on that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that was the case. He was the warden of the KP Dom, of the penitentiary, and it was within his jurisdiction, was the KP Dom as an entity, and there was only one man who acted as its warden. There were several so-called work units, work units or department or whatever they called them, and which before the war functioned as, say, a Work Unit Drina, and it was responsible for organising furniture production. It had its farm, it had its catering unit, it had its fishpond, and so on and so forth. It had different departments, but all of them were under the jurisdiction of the KP Dom warden, and they were all funded by the Republican budget through the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And one last question. You were asked about your meeting with Mr. Krnojelac when you were washing the carpets in the prison yard, and you mentioned in your evidence that you spoke to Mr. Krnojelac about -- with concerns about your uncle. My friend then asked you a question: "Later that same day, did Mr. Todovic" --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, maybe I'm putting the cart before the horse, but I do not think that such a question can be asked in redirect. But I see that my learned friend has -- is using it as an introduction to the next question, which was my question during the cross-examination. So perhaps I should wait for the question to be asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think that might be a good idea. You proceed with the evidence, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke to Mr. Krnojelac in the yard about your uncle, was Mr. Todovic there at that time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Todovic was not there at the time. He arrived some 10 or perhaps 15 minutes later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for His Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, you may now leave, but will you wait until the blinds have been pulled down, when you'll be escorted from the courtroom. Is Witness 182 the next one? We'll have to wait for that witness to be brought in. Apparently he or she has to be brought from some distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I am unaware, but my friend may be able to assist.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness is here in the house and just has to be brought in from the witness room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The usher warned me that it may take a few minutes, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The usual list of pseudonyms to which the witness will be referred to, headed "FWS-182," will be Exhibit P406 and it will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Will you please make the solemn declaration in the document that's being shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good day, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you speak a little bit louder so that the interpreters can hear your voice.

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: Very well. Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you have been granted the protective measure that you had requested, and you have a sheet of paper in front of you. No?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can the witness please be given the Exhibit 4 or 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This sheet in front of you, you see a number on top of it, the number 182. That's your pseudonym. Below this number there is a name. Is that your name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the date below this name, is that your birth date?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, on that same sheet you have three more names, and whenever you would like to refer to these people listed there, would you please not say the name but the number because these are also protected witnesses. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, where were you born?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: Bosniak Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have children?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: I have two children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you live before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: In Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in which neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: In the centre of Foca, the very centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your profession before the war? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: I was a technical producer in a particular organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "producer," that means you just have to do the technical matters related to the job or were you also a kind of reporter?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: I worked as a journalist for a different organisation and also for this organisation that I worked for from time to time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... session? I just wanted to ask, because I just wanted to ask him where he worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It would be quicker, would it not, if we just had it written down?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, but it's just one particular question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of any political party before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of party was it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: The Party of the Reformist Forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this in an ethnically mixed party?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it cooperate in any way with the SDA or the SDS?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: No way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say so vehemently, "No way"?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: Because it was not a nationalist party. It was a party that brought together the reformist forces. It was a party that focused on economic programmes. It is the party of the former Prime Minister of Yugoslavia, Ante Markovic who managed to bring about a recovery of Yugoslavia in an economic sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did your party not want to cooperate with the other two?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: Because pre-election rallies of these nationalist parties were already being held, it so happened that I followed these rallies of these parties. They wanted to make their own ethnic groups homogenous. However, we were multiethnic, so to speak. There were Serbs, Croats, members of all ethnic groups in our party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend any party meeting or assembly of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: In view of the job I had, I was duty-bound to do so from time to time and I did so, of course. Yes, I did attend the meetings of these parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the main position of the SDS towards other ethnic groups? Could you describe it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: First of all, they wanted to homogenise the people, so to speak, at these pre-election rallies; they wanted to organise the people in that way. They were blaming the communists, the reformists, the Bosniak people. They were saying that they had to take power because they were being threatened, that they faced the threat of being exterminated. Those were the major overtones. There was warmongering. It was like that, sort of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "they," you mean the Serbs were threatened, the Serb people were threatened?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any particular things they said, and who said that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: I remember at one such pre-election rally where Mr. Karadzic was present, Mr. Maksimovic, Mr. Ostojic, the late Koljevic, Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Kilibarda, they spoke in such a tone.
