utterances.text: Well, it was just a fleeting moment. But at that moment, I felt happy, I felt joy. After that I didn't, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said the guards came to call out detainees, did they have any piece of paper or even a written or typed list from which they called out detainees?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: I remember that. There was a small green piece of paper, small piece of green paper that Stefanovic had, and that is what they used to do when they take somebody away and then bring him back again with a similar piece of paper. But this small paper always came from the administrative building; that is, a guard would always come from the administrative building with such a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already mentioned that you heard the sounds of beating and screaming. Could you make out from which part of the administration building these sounds came from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: From that same part which I indicated when I showed you where it was that Mr. Krnojelac saw me, received me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you ever hear from the voices you heard who was beating a detainee? Did you ever hear something so specific that you could be sure who was beating?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: I'm 100 per cent sure about one particular case; about others, no. But on that one occasion, I heard a voice which I knew very well and which I'd often heard before. It was the voice of Rajko Cicmil, and I believe he died meanwhile. I did see him once in the compound, once in a uniform with an officer bag and pistol, and he had a cap. Not the officer's cap but a different kind of cap. I knew him because while I worked for a different organisation, he was my assistant for three years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Rajko Cicmil, was he a guard or was he a soldier?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: Military, he had a military uniform, same as Mr. Krnojelac when I saw him on that occasion, the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you hear him say or shout?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: He said, "Confess. Own up. Own up better or we'll kill you," shouted at him, and that was it. "Own up. Tell us where it is or --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure.

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: "-- we'll kill you." That is what stuck in my memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you hear whom he was beating? Did you hear from the answers or from the voices who was actually the victim of Mr. Cicmil?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: The victim could only moan and cry for help, and not very distinctly. Obviously, it must have been painful. His cries, his screams, you can't really distinguish -- I mean, of course you distinguish, you know what a scream is, you know what a cry of pain is, of course you do, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, you better have a look at the transcript. You'll see a passage there at line 18 -- 17 where the interpreters had some difficulty in understanding precisely what it was the witness was saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you have mentioned what you heard Mr. Cicmil shout, and we have in the transcript -- we lack a part. It says, "Own up. Tell us where it is or," and then the interpreters have lost you. What did you hear Mr. Cicmil shout?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: That is what he said, "You'd better own up where they are or else we'll kill you." "Better tell us where they are or else we'll kill you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that clarifies the matter. You have already started to tell us about specific victims. Now I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. can't see the transcript but I think you spoke about Zulfo Veiz, or am I mistaken? I can't see that now. Yes, I think you have already mentioned Zulfo Veiz, who was with you in your room, yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's Schedule C, number 29, and also in the indictment, it's 5.27, the incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, how often was Mr. Veiz -- Zulfo Veiz taken out? Was it only on this one occasion, or was he taken out and returned?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: Zulfo was taken out on several occasions and brought back. But then once when he was taken away, he did not return again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw him return, what did he look like? Could you see any injuries on him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: No, I did not see any injuries. No. He told us then why he had been called out. Zulfo Veiz used to work for the police before the war, and it was his fellow policemen who had come and were telling Zulfo's wife where he was and what his children were doing, and that is what Zulfo told us. He did not -- at least we couldn't see any injuries, any aftereffects.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you that he was beaten or did he keep quiet?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: I just said, he told us -- well, on at least one occasion he told me, not only me but everybody who was sitting around us, that his colleague had come to tell him, as I have told you, about his family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any other specific person that you remember that was taken out in this manner and was beaten or even disappeared?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: I remember those who were with me when we were arrested. And when we were arrested, I did not see it then because at that time I did not know that we were arrested by Gojko Jokanovic. I didn't know his name then; I learned it later. So that Halim Konjo, he had been with me at my sister's. Uzunovic was another who arrived with me and never returned then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me finish one after the other. You said Halim Konjo. What can you tell us about him? Was he taken out once or on several occasions? Did you see him being beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: Halim had been taken out even while we were at Brod, and he was with me at Brod too. They had taken all his money. He was quite well-off. They took all his money, and that is what happened while we were at Brod. Then they took him - at least that's what he told me - they took him to the army club in the town, that that is where they took him, but at that time there was a military or perhaps paramilitary police, I don't know, and that they also took him there and beat him. His nickname was Spona. Selimovic, I believe, was his last name, Spona, and they took him there together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to tell us what happened to these persons in the KP Dom, not so much before they arrived there but in the KP Dom. Was Mr. Halim Konjo beaten while in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: We did not share the same room, but once he left, he never came back, Halim, so that I cannot tell you anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This Konjo Halim, that's C13. And he also mentioned B33.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know or can you tell us what happened to Halid Konjo while in the KP Dom? Not before.

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: Halid Konjo. We lived there until exchange, and then he was taken for exchange and he did not come back. At least that is what we were told, that people who were being taken for exchange, unfortunately many of those who were taken for exchange are missing. But I do think that he was sent to pick plums or something. It was September or October, and he did not come back again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned already a detainee with the name Enes Uzunovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours this is Schedule C26, and also the incident 5.29.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Enes Uzunovic in the KP Dom? Was he taken out for beatings? Did you see him there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: Yes, I did see Uzunovic. He was badly beaten. After what I told you about that salt storage, that is how he looked too. He was all black and blue. And I saw him then on the stairs. He could not walk. That was the last time I saw him. That was, I think, sometime in late May. That is Uzunovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you saw him on the stairs. What does that mean? You saw him return from the administration building, on the staircase, or what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: From the administrative building --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. The witness did not say where he was coming back from. This is a leading question, whether he was returning from the administrative building. He only said he saw him on the stairs, and the next question was whether he saw him on the stairs as he was returning from the administrative building. That is a leading question. So presumably the question should be whether the witness saw him, where he was coming back from, and what stairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think that unless you heard something that the translators didn't hear, there is no reference to the administrative building there in the transcript, so you should ask him that question again. The damage may well have been done, but I think you should ask it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned that you saw him all black and blue, and you saw him on the stairs. Which stairs and where was he coming from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: Sorry. Stairs -- it is from that small garden. There are a couple of stairs, and this is right next to the administrative building. Ten metres -- no, perhaps 5 metres from the administrative building there is a slightly raised platform and there were stairs, and that is where one could see him very well on that corner. He simply was not able to walk any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see where he was coming from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: No, I did not see that. I saw him sitting down. But I did see people go through the door -- come out of the door, that is, he was pushed. The door opened, that is, that entrance into the administrative building. Mandzo, I think his name was, and I believe he was a male -- a lab assistant. I saw him. He was practically down on his knees and hands because he could not walk. They must have beaten them on the soles of his feet. And he once went through there and he barely made it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this is Mandzo that you mentioned you saw coming from the administration building?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the other one, this person we spoke about before, you did only see him on the stairs and you do not know where he came from. Did you see --

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him -- before you saw him on the stairs in this bad condition, did you see him go somewhere before that? Did you see him being led somewhere?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whom else do you recall belonging to this group of people who disappeared in this time period that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: I recall Matovic, a Croat, male nurse; Nail Hodzic; Nurko Nisic; and, yes, other people too. Some I knew by sight and some I knew better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Nail Hodzic. That is number C10. What did you see happened to Nail Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: I did not see anything. I only saw him being taken away, that is, when he went out of the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Croat Matovic that you mentioned, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: Yes, him too. He did not come back again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Nurko Nisic. You mentioned Nurko Nisic.

utterances.speaker: FWS-182
utterances.text: Nurko I did see as he was coming back from the administrative building. He had some sports clothes on him, some sweatsuits or something, and he was beaten up. He walked with difficulty, and he went by, but where he went -- and later on I heard that he was taken to solitary confinement and then out of there, taken again somewhere, but I don't know where.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is C29 and the incident 5.27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That may be enough. There are a couple of matters I wanted to raise with you before we adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now that the Defence has filed a supplement to their motion, you may want to deal with that. Could you deal with it overnight so that we've got the opportunity tomorrow to deal with it finally?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, but actually, we are also prepared to do that now, but whatever you prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think the translators have had a pretty hard day today, but if you'd like to state what your attitude is. Do you still object to the medical examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't understand what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: This is the motion that the Defence has put on to have their client examined, and you took the point, which was a good one, that they had never identified the issue to which the examination would be relevant. They've now done so. The question is: Do you still object to the appointment of an examiner? If you don't, do you want your own examiner appointed as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Actually, we want to oppose it in the way as it stands for the moment, because what they are actually requesting from you is to order a very specific and detailed examination, even giving the scope of the examination, and I think this has to be clarified because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Look, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I don't want to have to debate it here. If you want to put this in writing, then they can deal with it in writing in reply or they may be able to deal with it in the morning orally, but I think it's not the time to be going into detail about it. If you oppose it, let's see why you oppose it. The other matter was have you prepared that summons for the witness that both parties want to have brought in?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It is being prepared at the moment. It will be presented to you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well then. We will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now until 9.30 in the morning, but Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, would you please discuss your problems about this medical examination with counsel for the defendant so we can try and get some agreement. The Trial Chamber is minded to grant any such application provided there is a sufficient identification of an issue. If you are concerned about the examination which is sought, my own view -- I haven't discussed this with my colleagues, but my own view is it's better to have more than less. If you'll remember, there was a very similar examination made in the last trial. The result of it was quite extraordinary in many ways, but, nevertheless, it saved having to have more than one. So I suggest that you should not take too great an issue about that. If you want your own doctor to examine the defendant, that's a matter which the Defence counsel will have to consider, but we would certainly look favourably upon such an application. It can't be done only one way, in other words, if it's going to be a Tribunal examiner. All right. 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
